lines.text: Britain, Chile and Argentina all claim one piece of Antarctica. None can have it.
7 countries have cut this ice into slices, like a cake, from the South Pole.
Britain draws the first line, back in its empire days, a slice down from the tip of South America.
New Zealand follows, then France, then Australia, which takes the biggest slice of all.
Norway takes the slice facing Africa, just months before the Second World War.
Then Chile and Argentina draw theirs right across Britain's, and three flags land on one peninsula.
At Hope Bay, on the very tip, Argentine soldiers even fire shots over a British team's heads.
So who wins? In 1959, 12 nations sign a treaty in Washington, and every line on this map freezes.
No country grows its slice, no army builds a base, and no bomb is tested on the ice.
Today, 58 countries are in the treaty, and bases from many of them sit inside other countries' slices.
From 2048, the treaty's voting members can ask to rewrite the rules. But is every slice taken?
No. One slice, Marie Byrd Land, has no flag at all: no country claims it.
Nobody's, or cut up for good: which should it be? Until then, three countries keep claiming one slice.
